title: Checkpoint: Storing Data
subtitle: Apply data models, indexes, transactions, and replication across one storage design
objectives: Recall storage fundamentals cold, without the cue of knowing which unit a question came from
Connect indexes, transactions and replication into one story about a single write
Diagnose a concurrency bug that no single unit's material spells out for you

exercises.prompt: A read-heavy database leader is overloaded. Add two replicas and route stale-tolerant reads away from the leader.
exercises.afterStatus: REPLICAS · 15,000 reads/s each · leader keeps writes
exercises.why: Replicas can absorb stale-tolerant reads while the leader remains the write authority. Read-your-writes and freshness-sensitive operations need routing that accounts for replication lag.

exercises.prompt: You add an index to speed up a slow `SELECT`. Your `INSERT`s get slower. Why?
choices: The index locks the table on every write
Every `INSERT` must now write the row *and* update the index — a second structure to keep sorted
Indexes force a full table scan on write
It doesn't — that's a coincidence
exercises.why: A B-tree index is a separate ordered structure containing indexed values and row references. Each `INSERT` must update the table and every affected index; an index update can also split a full tree page. Additional indexes can accelerate matching reads while consuming storage and reducing write throughput, so each index should support a demonstrated query pattern.
exercises.hint: What else has to stay correct when a row appears?

exercises.prompt: Before touching the real data, the database appends a record of what it's about to do to a sequential ______ and forces *that* to disk.
choices: write-ahead log
index
replica
cache
exercises.why: The write-ahead log (WAL) records a change before the corresponding data pages are written. Appending and flushing the WAL establishes a durable recovery record; after a crash, the database replays committed log records whose data pages were not yet persisted. PostgreSQL can also stream WAL records to replicas, which replay the same changes in order.
exercises.hint: It's how a crash doesn't cost you an acknowledged write.

exercises.prompt: Your signup endpoint creates duplicate accounts under load. Which of these actually fix it? Select all.
choices: A `UNIQUE` constraint on `email`
`SELECT` to check the email is free, then `INSERT` if nothing came back
Wrapping that check-then-insert in a transaction at Read Committed
Running that check-then-insert at Serializable isolation
exercises.why: A `UNIQUE` constraint makes the database reject a second committed row with the same email, including when inserts race. At Read Committed, two transactions can both observe no row and then insert because the initial check does not reserve the missing value. PostgreSQL Serializable tracks predicate read/write dependencies and aborts one unsafe execution, which the application must retry; the constraint is the direct invariant and should still be present.
exercises.hint: Two requests, both looking before they leap, at exactly the same moment.

exercises.prompt: Your code runs the same `SELECT` twice inside one transaction and assumes it gets the same rows back. On Postgres, which isolation level are you assuming — and which do you get by default?
choices: Assuming Repeatable Read; you get Repeatable Read by default
Assuming Repeatable Read; but Postgres defaults to Read Committed, where each *statement* takes a fresh snapshot
Assuming Serializable; you get Serializable by default
Assuming Read Uncommitted; you get Read Uncommitted by default
exercises.why: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed, where each statement reads from a snapshot taken at the start of that statement. A transaction can therefore run the same `SELECT` twice and observe a value committed between the statements; this is a non-repeatable read. Repeatable Read uses one transaction snapshot, so code requiring stable repeated reads must request that level or enforce the invariant another way.
exercises.hint: The default is weaker than the thing you're assuming.

exercises.prompt: Match each replication term to what it means.

pairs.right: The leader waits for a follower before acknowledging
The leader can acknowledge after local durability without waiting for a follower
How far behind the leader a follower currently is
Promoting a follower when the leader is gone

exercises.why: With synchronous replication, the leader waits for the configured follower acknowledgement before reporting success, adding network and follower latency to the write path. With asynchronous replication, it does not wait for a follower, though it may still wait for its own write-ahead log to become durable. A promoted follower can therefore lack acknowledged writes that had not reached it. Replication lag measures that delay, and failover promotes a follower.
exercises.hint: Two of these are settings, one is a measurement, one is an event.

exercises.prompt: A read replica is 200ms behind. A user saves their profile, and the page reloads immediately. What can they see?
choices: Their new profile — the write already committed
Possibly their OLD profile, because the reload can land on a replica that hasn't applied the change yet
An error
The replica blocks the read until it catches up
exercises.why: The leader contains the committed profile update, while a replica that is 200ms behind still contains the previous version. If the reload is routed to that replica, the user can read the old profile and lose read-your-writes consistency. Systems that require this guarantee can temporarily route that user's reads to the leader or wait until a replica has applied at least the user's write position.
exercises.hint: Committed on the leader is not the same as visible where you're reading.

exercises.prompt: Wire a leader–follower setup: writes must land in one place, and that place ships its log onward.
exercises.why: In leader–follower replication, clients send writes to the leader, which establishes their order and records them in its log. Followers receive and replay that log, and may serve reads after applying entries. Sending reads to asynchronously updated followers adds read capacity while permitting stale results; accepting writes at multiple leaders would require a separate conflict-detection and resolution design.
exercises.hint: Which box can never be wrong about the order of writes?

exercises.prompt: Your leader tops out at 5,000 req/s. Read traffic is 30,000 req/s. Drag reads onto replicas until the leader survives — using the *smallest* share you can.

absorb.label: Share of reads sent to replicas

exercises.why: At whole-percent precision, 83% still leaves 5,100 reads/second on the leader and exceeds its 5,000-request/second capacity. Sending the smallest valid share, 84%, to replicas leaves 16%, or 4,800 reads/second, on the leader. Replica routing should still be selected by freshness requirement.
exercises.hint: The leader's limit is fixed. The only free variable is what fraction never reaches it.

exercises.prompt: Your code does: `BEGIN` · `SELECT balance` (100) · your app computes `100 - 10` · `UPDATE balance = 90` · `COMMIT`. Two of these run at once at Read Committed. What happens?
choices: The database serializes them; the balance ends at 80
Lost update: both read 100, both write 90, and one withdrawal silently vanishes
One transaction gets a deadlock error
Read Committed prevents this
exercises.why: Both transactions can read 100, compute 90 independently, and then write the same value, leaving a final balance of 90 after two withdrawals. This lost update occurs because the application writes a stale computed value. An atomic relative update such as `SET balance = balance - 10`, a row lock acquired before reading, or an isolation level that detects the conflicting update can preserve both changes; aborted transactions must be retried.
exercises.hint: Where does the subtraction actually happen?

exercises.prompt: Every write in your system takes this path. Where's the ceiling?
exercises.why: Every write passes through the leader, whose 5,000-writes/second capacity is the lowest in the path. Followers can replay 9,000 writes/second, leaving 4,000 writes/second of replay headroom while the leader is saturated. If follower replay capacity falls below the leader's write rate, unapplied log entries accumulate and replication lag grows until replay again exceeds incoming writes.
exercises.hint: Adding app servers can't help you past a number further down.

exercises.prompt: A B-tree with fanout 500 can address about 125 million entries at three levels and 62.5 billion at four. A table has 1 billion rows. What does this imply for an indexed point lookup?
choices: The index needs four levels, so the lookup follows about four tree pages before reaching the row reference
The index must scan all 1 billion entries
The index needs hundreds of levels because the table has a billion rows
The index cannot represent a table larger than 125 million rows
exercises.why: Three levels cover only 125 million entries, while four cover 62.5 billion, so 1 billion entries require about four B-tree levels. A point lookup follows one branch per level, and upper pages are frequently cached because many lookups reuse them. High fanout keeps tree depth small as the table grows; query performance still depends on selectivity, page caching, and whether the query can use the index.
exercises.hint: Use the supplied capacities and choose the first depth that covers 1 billion rows.

exercises.prompt: You arrived at this tier believing a database 'just works'. What has it actually shown you?
choices: Databases are unreliable and you should avoid them
A database is a stack of promises you *configure* — durability, isolation, freshness — and every default trades one of them for speed
You should always use the strongest setting available
NoSQL avoids all of this
exercises.why: Database behavior depends on configured guarantees. Isolation determines which concurrent histories are allowed, commit settings determine when durability is acknowledged, and replication mode determines when copies receive a write. Stronger settings add coordination, latency, blocking, or retries. Each application invariant and freshness requirement therefore needs an explicit matching guarantee and configuration.
exercises.hint: Every default in this tier was someone choosing speed on your behalf.

exercises.prompt: A hospital writes a prescription transactionally to the leader, then a dashboard reads an asynchronous follower and briefly misses it. Which two properties are involved?
choices: Atomic leader commit and replica freshness
DNS and CDN caching
Shard-key selection and rate limiting
HTTP safety and UDP ordering
exercises.why: The authoritative transaction can commit atomically while an asynchronous copy still lags. Transaction atomicity and replica freshness are separate guarantees.
